---
title: "5 Methodological randomized study"
link-citations: true
---

Alternative labels: methodological trial; randomized methodological comparison

## Definition and features
In methodological randomized studies, researchers treat methods as interventions. They randomize individual humans (such as researchers, research participants, peer reviewers, or methods users) or groups of humans (such as study teams, consensus panels, or research environments) to apply, consider, or receive training in one or more alternative methods. They then measure outcomes such as effect estimates, study processes (such as recruitment or retention), or characteristics of study reports (such as clarity, completeness, or use of appropriate methods). This type includes randomized studies embedded within other studies.

- A strength of randomised studies is that they allow causal conclusions about methodological interventions as humans understand and implement them under realistic conditions. 
- A limitation is feasibility, especially when interventions target studies or research environments rather than individual researchers or study participants.

## Typical purposes and corresponding examples 
[Compare two or more methods](../purposes/8compare-methods.qmd): Does a central study team improve recruitment (study within a trial)?[@OtherOtherswat] Do different incentives affect investigators’ sharing of individual participant data (study within a review)?[@OtherOtherswar] Which version of an evidence table is easier to understand for guideline users?[@Carrasco-Labra2016improving] Does reminding peer reviewers of reporting items improve study reports?[@Speich2023reminding]
